content: The Health-Promoting Schools (HPS) initiative has the potential to drive significant changes in schools by integrating health promotion into national strategic planning. This includes the systematic collection and monitoring of data to ensure effective implementation. The guidance for implementing HPS aligns with global standards and indicators, which envision all schools worldwide enhancing the health, well-being, and educational outcomes of their students and communities. To achieve this, schools must adopt a comprehensive, whole-school approach to health promotion. This approach goes beyond isolated health topics or programs and incorporates the school’s culture, conditions, and curriculum into a cohesive HPS system. The eight global standards for sustainable HPS systems provide a framework for this transformation, supporting schools in creating environments that promote health and well-being. Stakeholder analysis and progress tracking are critical components of HPS implementation. Tools such as stakeholder mapping can help identify the impact and influence of various groups on HPS activities. This analysis determines the extent to which HPS will affect each stakeholder group and their influence on the outcomes. Based on this, appropriate engagement strategies can be developed, such as providing regular updates to stakeholders with moderate influence or actively collaborating with those who have strong influence and are directly affected by HPS. Stakeholders with significant influence and direct involvement in HPS should play an active role in its implementation. Conversely, stakeholders with limited influence and indirect involvement may be monitored and informed about progress when they show interest. Identifying relevant stakeholders is a dynamic process, as their involvement may vary depending on the focus of the implementation at different stages. For example, senior government leaders may be heavily involved during policy development but take on a more consultative role once a national education policy and coordination group are established. Stakeholders with mandated responsibilities, such as reviewing school infrastructure, should be consistently engaged throughout the process. Periodic involvement of other stakeholders can be determined through stakeholder mapping and by addressing key questions, such as identifying those with direct or indirect influence, those interested in HPS at various levels, and those with relevant experience or expertise. The implementation of HPS requires the use of appropriate methods for engaging stakeholders, including thorough documentation. Resources and tools for stakeholder analysis and engagement are available to guide this process. These tools help ensure that all relevant parties are involved in planning, monitoring, and evaluating HPS activities, ultimately contributing to the success and sustainability of health-promoting schools.
